summary: At the Moon's south pole the Sun circles the horizon and never rises, so a distant ridge can hide the Sun, or Earth, for days. A lander needs both: sunlight for power and Earth in view for its radio link. LUNAR EXPLORER lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and start dates in seconds. Pick a site, a date and a stay length; the tool computes the site's real horizon from NASA LOLA elevations, checks hour by hour whether the Sun and Earth are above it using NASA JPL Horizons positions, and returns a clear verdict: go, review or no-go. It then suggests a better date or site. Example: at Connecting Ridge, starting 16 days earlier raises Earth visibility from 18% to 98% at the same site. Every number shows its law, its data source and its confidence. Our computed sunlight map agrees with NASA's published map (correlation 0.987 over the full map), and anyone can rerun a live check inside the tool. It runs in any browser, in English and Arabic.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
One sentence drives the tool: "I want to land at [site] on [date] for [days] with a [vehicle]". It answers with a decision board: sunlight %, Earth-link %, longest darkness, slope, survival battery and distance to the nearest likely cold trap, each coloured green, yellow or red. A timeline shows Sun and Earth visibility hour by hour, and a 360° horizon plot shows where each one clears the terrain.

HOW IT WORKS
1. Horizon: for each site we scan LOLA elevations in every direction, with lunar curvature, to get the true horizon angle.
2. Geometry: hourly Sun and Earth positions for 2027-2028 from NASA JPL Horizons.
3. Visibility: the Sun counts as visible when more than half its disc is above the horizon; Earth when it is above the horizon (line of sight).
4. Decision: power, battery for the longest darkness, and link windows are combined into go / review / no-go, with a suggested better date or site.

WHAT ELSE IT OFFERS
Seven candidate sites including the IM-2 landing area, any point you click, rover routes with alternatives and an animated trip, side-by-side comparison of sites and dates, a solar-versus-RTG comparison, map layers (sunlight over the year, longest darkness, Earth link, slope, ice-stability index, permanent shadow), a printable scientific report, a 5-step guided tour, and a user guide in English and Arabic.

VALIDATION
- Our computed sunlight map against NASA's published map over 1.1 million cells: correlation 0.987, mean difference 3.0 percentage points.
- A live test of 300 random points that anyone can run inside the tool; each run draws new points (a typical run gives a correlation of about 0.97).
- Sun and Earth elevation within about 0.001° of JPL Horizons on 13 dates (azimuth within 0.01°).
- 99.9% of NASA's mapped permanent shadow falls inside ours; our shadow area is larger, so the tool errs on the dark side.
The tool also lists what it does not know.

IMPACT
Mission planners and CLPS teams can see the longest darkness and link outage before they become a failed mission. Teachers get one file that works offline in two languages, with every term and law explained on click.

CREATIVITY
The date matters as much as the place: the same site goes from 18% to 98% Earth visibility by moving the start 16 days. The tool makes that visible, and proves its own numbers against NASA's in front of the user.

TOOLS
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no server, one self-contained file); Python for data preparation; GitHub Pages for hosting.
dataRefs: NASA GSFC PGDA Lunar Polar Illumination (AVGVISIB, LPSR)
projectRefs: Mazarico et al. 2011, Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions (NASA NTRS)
